chapter: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
title: Two trips to Japan
summary: He describes fast taxis, bullet train, solar roofs, and how Japan became money-conscious between his visits.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: You went to Japan with the group, didn't you?

The early '60's and then a couple of years, went again. Was really beautiful. When I first went over there, it seemed that the people weren't too used to Americans at that time, and they were very interested, and they had some beautiful hotels. They're beautiful people. We were at some lovely places. And they had some little incidents that were particularly notable. One is the taxi drivers in Tokyo.

I never saw so many taxicabs go so fast in my life. So you sit on the edge of the seat waiting for the crash, and if a taxicab is damaged, like in the morning. When you see that taxicab that afternoon, it's back on the street, perfect condition, --
-- which I thought of at the time, we could use a little of that over here.

And, of course, we did some traveling up into Japan. We rode that fast, fast train, which is something to see. You come to a station, and before you can see the station, you're gone. The station is back there somewhere. And I think we saw -- we saw that monorail. And also I was quite interested, especially lately. When we were in Japan several years ago there was quite a lot of use of solar system, especially out in the country. You'd see these -- look like glass windows laying on top of the house, on the side, and that was a solar system. And it seems that it's just now taking hold over here, when that's an old thing over there. Saw it a long time ago.

And they have some very interesting buildings, and the audiences are very nice. And they had a thing too that was interesting in their employment situation. The first time we went to Japan, as I said, they had these very beautiful hotels and stores and places like that. But they had a system -- like if your store would only -- should only require ten people employed, they had 15 employed and would split the moneys down so that everybody had some employment and some money, which I thought was a terrific idea, but they were doing it quite a while ago.

Now, the second time we went back, it had gotten a little more -- well, money was the thing. They were very money-conscious, and there weren't too many places where you even saw the old, colloquial dress. They didn't -- you know,

the coolie clothes or the coolie pants. Everything was western -- western -- and everything costs a lot of money. We stayed in a -- first time in a very beautiful hotel -- W: Otani, I think. [Otani -- Oritani] Hotel? B: Yeah, it was really just like any big western hotel, very beautiful, very well appointed, all of the stores and shops, and the next time it's a little higher, little higher, and I didn't go the third time. That's when I quit in 1970. They left the next day and went back to Japan.

But it's interesting to see the changes that come over countries. But it seems the trend is mostly getting to the western ideas, which is money. I even remember in Sweden and those countries, when we first went over there, it was a more relaxed -- but now everything's getting so tight and hurried -- everybody hurries, see. So I guess we'll all be of one nature pretty soon. There won't be any --
